client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. It's like this heavy sadness just sits on my chest all day, and I can't seem to focus on anything — even simple things like making breakfast or answering emails feel impossible. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, and I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief like this can make even the smallest tasks feel like mountains, and what you're describing makes complete sense. I notice there's a quiet heaviness in how you're sharing this, like the weight of it goes even deeper than words can quite capture right now. It takes courage to show up when part of you isn't sure it will help — can you tell me a little more about what your days have been feeling like since she passed?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, my days feel kind of hollow. I wake up and for just a second everything feels normal, and then it hits me all over again and I just... don't really see the point in doing much. I've also been feeling guilty, like I should have called her more in the last few months, and that guilt just makes the sadness even heavier.
therapist: That moment of waking up and briefly forgetting, then having it rush back — that's one of the most painful parts of grief, and it makes so much sense that it leaves you feeling hollow. I'm also noticing that as you talk about this, there's something that sounds almost hurried beneath the quietness — like there's a lot more feeling moving through you than you might be letting fully land. That guilt you're carrying about not calling more — where does that voice come from, and how long has it been speaking to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That guilt voice has honestly been there for a while, not just since she died. I was always kind of telling myself I'd call her "next week" and then next week would come and go, and now there is no next week and I can't fix it. I guess the voice got a lot louder after she passed, like it's trying to remind me constantly that I had chances and didn't take them.
therapist: That "next week" pattern is something so many of us fall into, and there's something quietly heartbreaking about the way you're describing it — like you're carrying not just the loss of her, but the loss of all those imagined future moments too. I'm curious: when that guilt voice speaks up, does it ever leave any room for the part of you that did love her, even when life got in the way of calling? Because love and imperfection can exist in the same relationship, and I wonder what it might feel like to gently hold both of those truths at once.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I want to believe that, but it feels almost too easy, like I'm just letting myself off the hook. The guilt voice is so loud that when I try to think about the love part, it kind of... drowns it out, you know? I'm not sure I've earned the right to hold both of those things together yet.
therapist: The way you said that — "I haven't earned the right" — struck me, because there's something that sounds almost urgent beneath those words, like a part of you is working very hard to hold something down. I want to gently push back on the idea that compassion toward yourself is the same as letting yourself off the hook — guilt this loud and persistent isn't protecting your grandmother's memory, it's actually keeping you from fully grieving her. What do you think she would say if she could hear the way you're speaking about yourself right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I know she wouldn't have wanted me to beat myself up like this — she was always pretty gentle with me, actually. But then part of me thinks that's exactly why it hurts so much, because she would have forgiven me easily and I'm not sure I can do the same for myself. It feels weird to use her kindness as a reason to be kinder to myself, like I'm borrowing something I didn't earn.
therapist: What you just shared is really profound — you already *know* how she would have responded to you, and that knowledge lives somewhere inside you, which means her gentleness isn't really borrowed, it's something she gave you that's already yours to keep. I'm also noticing that even as you're talking about her softness, there's an energy in your voice that sounds almost urgent or pressured, like part of you is fighting hard against letting this realization fully land. What would it feel like to just sit with the possibility, even for a moment, that forgiving yourself might actually be a way of honoring her rather than taking something you didn't earn?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: That framing actually caught me off guard a little, because I hadn't thought of it that way — like forgiving myself could be something for her, not just for me. But I'm also a little wary, because it sounds like something that makes sense in this room right now and then falls apart the moment I'm alone at home and the guilt comes rushing back. I guess I just don't trust that a new way of thinking about it will hold up when I'm in the middle of a really bad moment.
therapist: That concern is actually really wise and worth taking seriously — insights that feel meaningful in a safe space can be hard to hold onto when you're alone at 2am and the guilt is loud. What we can do together is build something more like a practice than a single realization, so that when those hard moments come, you have something concrete to reach for rather than relying on a feeling that might fade. Can you think of a time in the past when you've managed to hold onto something difficult but true about yourself, even when a louder voice was pushing back?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I'm trying to think of an example and it's actually harder than I expected, which makes me feel a little embarrassed. Maybe when I went through a rough patch at work a few years ago, I kept reminding myself I was capable even when I felt like a failure, and eventually it did help — but that felt different because it was about me, not about someone I lost. I guess I'm not sure the same kind of self-talk would work when the grief and guilt are this tangled together.
therapist: Please don't feel embarrassed — you just pulled up a really meaningful example, and it actually tells us something important: you *have* talked yourself through darkness before, even when it felt impossible. You're right that grief is different from a work struggle, but the skill you used then — holding onto something true about yourself against a loud opposing voice — is the same muscle we'd be working with here, just applied to a harder situation. I'm wondering if we could start small: what's one true thing about your relationship with your grandmother that the guilt voice can't actually take away from you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think... she knew I loved her. Even if I didn't call as often as I should have, when we did talk it was real, and she used to tell me that hearing my voice made her day. The guilt voice is already trying to argue with that, telling me that it wasn't enough, but I can see that it's at least partly true in a way that's hard to completely dismiss.
therapist: What you just said — "she knew I loved her" — that's not a small thing, and I want you to notice that you found it even with the guilt voice pushing back in real time, which means it's strong enough to hold its ground. I also notice something in how you said it, a kind of rushing quality, like you wanted to get it out quickly before the doubt could catch up — and I wonder if slowing down and really letting that truth settle might feel different than just saying it. Can you say it once more, a little slower, and just notice what happens in your body when you do?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: She knew I loved her. I said it slower that time and it's strange, because there was this brief moment where the guilt kind of... quieted, just slightly, and I felt something sad but also almost warm in my chest. But now I'm already worrying that I'm just going to forget this feeling the second I leave here, which I know is probably me getting in my own way again.
therapist: What you just experienced — that brief quieting, that sad-but-warm feeling — that's not nothing, that's actually your nervous system recognizing something true, and it's worth trusting that it happened even if it felt fleeting. You're right that you might not carry the feeling perfectly, but you don't need to — what you *can* carry is the memory that you found it once, which means you can find it again. What if, between now and our next conversation, you just practiced saying that one sentence to yourself once a day, not to fix anything, but just to keep the door to it open?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Once a day feels manageable, I think, but I'm a little worried about what happens when I say it and the guilt voice just immediately shouts it down and I end up feeling worse than before I tried. Like, what do I do in that moment — do I just push through it, or is there something else I'm supposed to do with the guilt when it shows up that loudly? I don't want to set myself up to fail at the one small thing you're asking me to try.
therapist: That's such a smart question to ask, and it tells me you're already thinking like someone who wants this to actually work rather than just sound good in theory. When the guilt voice shouts back, the goal isn't to out-argue it or push through it — instead, try just noticing it, almost like saying to yourself "there's that voice again," and then gently returning to the true thing, the way you might refocus after a distraction without judging yourself for drifting. You're not failing if the guilt shows up — you're only practicing, and practicing means it gets messy sometimes.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
